utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. There were a few minor matters which we have to address. Mr. Misetic was there something you would like to put on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President we were asked to clarify from our argument at draft transcript page 8, lines 7 to 9, concerning the footnote references to General Jones's cross-examination. Our position is that the Prosecution's case on necessary and reasonable measures through trial is as outlined in paragraph 605 of our brief and then the specific portions of that which were put to General Jones are at footnotes 1048, 1050 and 1051. And the other correction is at draft transcript page 9, lines 11 to 14, I had misspoken as to the elements of command responsibility that need to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. Those elements are at paragraph 609 of our brief and it is our position that each of the elements must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Mr. Tieger, some mistakes to be corrected for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. We'd like to make one correction to the record from the submissions on Monday and that would be the reference at transcript page 29, 118, line 5, and that's to Exhibit P1142. Which should in fact be a reference to Exhibit P1141.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. Then I would like to put on the record that we had a delayed start today due to the non-functioning of LiveNote on our computers. The Chamber considered it's wiser, especially since closing argument is important, not to start just with records but not accessible for us to make any annotations. That's the reason why we had a late start. And there a few matters, and I take it that the phosphoric shells will find their way through argument today. Mr. Tieger, to the extent I have not been clear, I intended -- I felt that yesterday you -- no, the day before yesterday, that there was insufficient time to make a general closing observation and you'll have an opportunity to and take whenever you have some -- need some -- an extra five or ten minutes for that, you have an opportunity to do that today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. I don't, at this point, intend to -- I wanted to concentrate on the rebuttal primarily, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but I wanted to express my gratitude to the Court for that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Kay, I do understand that you distributed a list of footnotes to the other parties. Has it been sent to the Chamber already or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not to the Chamber. To the other parties first and then when we have their agreement, we would then send it to the Chamber, with Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the other parties are invited to look at that rather quickly so that the Chamber has access to the list of footnotes, or give an unlimited consent already at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Finally, a feature not found in our Rules but, at the same time, not uncommon in this Tribunal is to give the accused an opportunity to briefly address the Court at the end of the hearings. No applications are made for such brief statements. These are usually unsworn statements and very much in line with, I would say, the civil law tradition of the last word for the accused. No applications have been made but if the accused would wish to apply for such an opportunity, the Chamber would be sympathetic to granting it. That's what I have on my agenda at this moment. Mr. Tieger, is the Prosecution ready to present its rebuttal final argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. And, Mr. President, perhaps we can begin with a matter that the Court raised and that's the issue of the phosphoric shells. The Court is aware of the context in which this arose. That was a claim by the Gotovina Defence asserting that it was incorrect to assert that General Gotovina took steps to conceal his subordinates' crimes at Grahovo by ordering report through a messenger that Glamoc and Grahovo were shelled, citing in particular Exhibit D1980 and the Mladic diary at the 2nd of August. I wanted to address that matter initially, Your Honour. The report that General Gotovina ordered was false, both in the narrow sense and in the broader sense. In the narrow sense, let's look at the two exhibits upon which the Defence relies. D1980 refers to phosphorous shells fired on the "woods at Staretina" on July 27th, and in that connection I would like to direct your attention to the map, place it on the screen. That's a map that's cropped from P2417. And as you can see at the bottom right, circled is Glamoc; the circle to the far left is Grahovo; and the circle to the top left is Drvar. The oval is the general area of the Staretina mountains and by way of -- I'm going to indicate, Your Honour, by way of scale, this is a map that's taken from two maps. The larger blocks to the right are approximately -- indicate about 4 kilometres horizontally and vertically, and the ones to the left about 2 kilometres. In any event, as you can see, the Staretina mountains and the Staretina woods are some distance away and calculated about 9 kilometres from the town of Glamoc. Grahovo, of course, is quite far away. And it is clear that no shells that were hitting the Staretina woods would have had an impact on Grahovo or Glamoc. As far as the Mladic diary is concerned, that's an entry of the 2nd of August: "The enemy burned the villages on the approaches to Glamoc and Grahovo and yesterday they started burning Grahovo. They are burning some of the villages from Grahovo to Drvar with incendiary artillery ammunition." Now as the Court will recall, the Split Military District forces had already occupied Grahovo on 28th of July, and it was clearly not shelling its own units in Grahovo. In any event, this postdates the period of time when the entire Grahovo was burning, as indicated by the Split Military District diary. So apart from the interesting information that villages are being burned from Grahovo to Drvar, that is not relevant to the issue of the report, and it's in that sense, that narrow sense, that the report that was issued is false. But more importantly, Your Honour, even if it technically been true in some respect, it was false in this sense. It was intended, clearly, to cover up what was really happening in Grahovo and what had really happened in Grahovo which was that most of the units, all but two, were involved in the destruction of Grahovo. And what happened, as the Court is aware from the evidence, is that at a Split Military District working meeting, the political department suggested that journalists not be permitted to come to Grahovo and that cameras be controlled, and General Gotovina ordered to report through a messenger that Glamoc and Grahovo were shelled by phosphoric shells, clearly to explain the destruction, should journalists somehow manage to become aware of that. That was cited by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The context is clear. What I was mainly seeking is further details as to the evidence whether phosphoric shells were used or not, which, of course, is irrelevant for is whether the report is false or not. You have explained that by drawing our attention to the fact that what there is in evidence about the use of phosphoric shells could not reasonably be interpreted as being related to Grahovo and Glamoc, and apart from that, that the other evidence rather goes in a different direction, because in order to establish that something is not there means that we need that all -- that there are no positive indications neither negative indications. That's clear. Thank you for that answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to turn next to some comments yesterday by the Markac Defence with respect to Mr. Janic. That would be found at transcript 122, 13, through 123, 19. And the Markac Defence indicated that Mr. Janic was never asked about Gracac and, in addition, indicated that -- well, I'll turn to that in a moment. The assertion was that he was never asked. In that respect, I would note that this is, in fact, contradicted by Mr. Janic's testimony at T6355 through 56. That's explicitly cited in the Prosecution's brief at footnote 2108. Mr. Janic said in response to a question about Gracac: "I know that near the town there were some military depots that were legitimate targets but the town itself wasn't and there was no fighting inside it, and there were no artillery strikes targeting the town." In addition, the Markac Defence stated that Mr. Russo had ignored other alleged key evidence about the shelling of Gracac, including Exhibit P102, that's an UNMO report, which they stated: "Reports that 15 shells fell in the area of Gracac on August 4th." In fact what the UNMO report states - and that should be on the screen now - is that the shells fell not in the area of Gracac but in Gracac town. And more importantly, Your Honour, these 15 rounds did not represent the sum total of shells fired at the town but were recorded between 2.00 p.m. and 5.00 p.m. on the afternoon of the 4th of August. That's nine hours after the shelling attack on Gracac began. So contrary to the assertions of the Markac Defence, this exhibit does not contradict but is completely consistent with the evidence of witnesses such as UNMO team leader Steenbergen and local resident Vida Gacesa that tens of shells fell -- landed in Gracac in the morning of the 4th of August. Let me turn next to an issue raised by the Gotovina Defence and the Markac Defence, both of whom suggested that the unlawfulness of the artillery attack was belied by General Forand and his presentation in 1996 asserting that the use of HV artillery was "excellent." And that was found at transcript pages 32, and 123 through 24, respectively. I think it's fair to say that based on his testimony that General Forand could not be pleased to hear that he is being invoked on behalf of the alleged legality of this shelling. The suggestion that he believed, either at the time he observed the shelling or later, that it was lawful is contradicted by his testimony before this Chamber, and that would be found at P331, P333, and transcript 4114 through 5, by his statements at the time of the shelling, P83, P341, and in fact by his statements in the very same presentation that the Defence relies upon. That's P401, in which he described "heavy barrages on towns and villages." That's at page 22. That the HV shelled UN observation posts in an effort to stop their reporting; page 28 and page 30. And that there was heavy shelling of Knin on the 5th of August, when Knin "was undefended and virtually empty." And finally, as General Forand explained in his statement at P330, page 4: "Their use of artillery was excellent when being used against military targets. However, the artillery was to a large extent used against villages and towns like Knin and not against targets in the zone of separation. This shelling created mass panic among the population and forced it to flee." A related matter, Your Honour, is the assertion by the Gotovina Defence that the illegality of shelling was inconsistent contemporaneous observations and that to believe the Prosecution's case you would have to believe, for example, that the eyes of the ARSK intelligence on the 4th of August were deceiving them. The Gotovina Defence, at transcript 29188, said that D389, in that document, the ARSK reported that the artillery attack was concentrated against the northern barracks, the ARSK command, the Tvik factory, the railway station, and others. What was not read from this document was the remainder, which indicates that the fire was directed at "the Kaplara barracks, the Tvik factory, the railway junction, residential buildings at the foot of the Knin fortress and elsewhere." Yesterday, Your Honour, the Gotovina Defence asserted that because the Prosecution has not produced photographs of Knin in rubble or evidence of massive deaths due to shelling, it has not established unlawful shelling. Indeed, the Gotovina Defence, at T58, accused the Prosecution of failing to produce evidence of an image it conjured up: "Stalingrad in the Second World War." Now this grossly misrepresented this threshold by which a shelling attack is considered to be without grounds in international law, and I would remind the Court that at the very commencement of this case, the Prosecution stated explicitly: "This was not Stalingrad or Vukovar, where weeks of shelling reduced the city to rubble. It was not the most destructive shelling of the war," but that is precisely the point. The intention was not to destroy Knin, the city of Zvonimir, into which President Tudjman intended to resettle Croats, but to drive out Serbs. Your Honours, the absence of concentrated damage and buildings in rubble is wholly consistent with the Prosecution's case that more than 1.000 projectiles were fired into Knin but were not directed at military objectives but, instead, widely dispersed throughout the city. A single rocket or shell impact, as the Court has learned, and I would cite the Court to Konings, T14314 through 15, will not demolish a building. And that's also reflected in the evidence of UNMOs such as Kari Anttila, who said that in the months after Storm, "it was possible to find out more locations where artillery and mortar shells had landed," and that based on these observations it is obvious that shelling did not concentrate against military objectives; P171, paragraph 3. Indeed, Your Honours, if the thousand projectiles were concentrated, we just might have photographs or reports of the ARSK headquarters or the northern barracks or the post office or other alleged military objectives in rubble, but that was not the case. Now the Gotovina Defence asserted that this slide used by Mr. Russo showing that shells were observed landing all over Knin was probative of virtually nothing. They asserted that the Chamber would need to know the concentration of fire of objects within these circles for it to be probative of anything. Your Honours, over one thousand shells were fired into Knin by HV forces. For argument's sake, even if 100 of these shells impacted military objectives, something that is not asserted -- not supported by the evidence as detailed at paragraphs 550 and 556 of the Prosecution's brief, that still leaves 900 projectiles landing throughout Knin within those red circles, and that is a breach of the principle of distinction. Indeed as Professor Corn, who's been cited, said at transcript 21509 of his testimony: "Where you say one rounds hits what's been identified as a high-value target, and this is the extreme hypothetical, if you could show that 900 other rounds hit civilian population centres while military objectives were ignored, I don't think you would need too much more corroboration of that circumstantial evidence." Further, Your Honour, the Gotovina Defence asserts at T3117 that the Prosecution's case must fail for lack of dozens of crater analyses. Now, the link between crater analyses and proving the illegality is unclear. Crater analyses are intended to determine the origin of fire. They are used in situations in which it is not clear which warring faction is responsible for firing the projectile. The Defence has never alleged that the HV were not responsible for an artillery attack on Knin. Indeed, evidence from observers, HV reports, General Gotovina's chief of artillery, and General Gotovina himself in his book, show that the HV were responsible for shelling Knin and the other towns in the attack order, rendering crater analyses superfluous. There is no question that more than one thousand projectiles landed -- listed in the HV expenditure reports were fired on Knin, and those are listed in footnote 1993. And those were, in fact, were fired by the HV. The Defence argue that the crater analysis in evidence shows that the ARSK fired rockets into Knin. Prosecution addresses the relevancy and accuracy of this assertion at paragraph 602 through 605 of its brief. Yesterday, the Defence argued that Oganj rocket could not have been fired by HV forces from the seized position at Vrhpolje because it was implausible that HV forces would be firing on Knin at that time. However, as the Gotovina Defence pointed out, the HV seized the Oganj weapon at 0855 - that's 8.55 a.m. - and HV troops did not begin to enter Knin until 10.00 a.m., leaving the HV over an hour to fire Oganj rockets into Knin. And the shelling of Knin by HV forces continued until approximately 11.00 a.m. See, for example, P695, paragraph 33. The Defence's alternative suggestion is unreasonable, given their continued reliance on D89, an UNCRO report that at 1800 hours on the 5th of August, there was an ARSK tank and mortar fire from Strmica "towards Knin." Now, this evidence is stretched to argue that it substantiates Oganj rocket fire. Not just towards Knin but on Knin. And that argument would require the Chamber to believe that the UNCRO observer confused mortar and tank fire for an Oganj rocket-launcher, and that rocket fire landed in Knin at 6.00 p.m. on the 5th of August, but no one, not the HV, nor the UN, observed or recorded such fire. Maybe it's the Prosecution's turn to raise Occam's Razor. In a situation where everyone who observes or is subjected to this artillery attack or recognises, as it's happening, that it is directed at civilians and civilian areas, where it is then found that that attack was the result of an order that said, Shell the towns, where subsequently a record of the meeting that trigged that order indicates that the subject of civilian flight triggered by shelling was important, when there's the use of weapons that can't discriminate between military targets and civilian areas under the circumstances, when the commander of the operation writes about the operation but omits to mention the use of the most indiscriminate weapons, when the Supreme Commander of the military forces is a person committed to the idea that too many Serbs in Croatia is a danger to the long-term sustainability of that nation, where there are efforts to keep those people out afterwards, the simplest solution to what happened seems quite clear. The Defence, Your Honour, cited with some interest and noted to the Court paragraph 7 of the Prosecution's brief which referred to an effort to plausibly deny, plausible deniability, and that was somehow turned into the idea of invisible ethnic cleansing. We would suggest to the Court that plausible deniability was quite rooted in the approach by Croatian authorities. Plausible deniability or pretext. And in that respect, the Court need only turn to the psy-ops "ostensibly guaranteeing civil rights." The Markac shelling which was to be a pretext discussed in P461. Obstacles to return. I have already shown you an exhibit during our presentation referring to it as a pretext, and the Court is aware of other evidence demonstrating that. The mask about negotiations that President Tudjman referred to in P461; the report about the phosphoric shells we have just looked at, and on and on. Plausible deniability, as we've seen, is pervasive throughout some of the efforts in this case. Another matter, Your Honour, yesterday the Gotovina Defence argued that it would have amounted to a "military coup d'etat against a civilian government" if General Gotovina had imposed a military curfew in Croatia. Now that was in reference to Prosecution's use of P1142. That's General Gotovina's military curfew order in Jajce, cited in footnote 642 as an example of one of the measures that General Gotovina could have but failed to take to prevent HV crimes in the Krajina. Let me show you quickly what P1142 states, just to remind you. "During this time I prohibit the individual movement of members of the Croatian forces in the street and at other public locations." This order, Your Honours, has nothing to do with civilian government. There's no reason he could not have imposed a similar measure in the Krajina. It's an order imposed on his subordinates to address "the increasing undisciplined conduct of members of the Croatian forces in the town of Jajce," and "for the purpose of creating conditions for the return of citizens." Your Honours, I would like to turn next to the insistence by the Gotovina Defence yesterday that the Chamber "must conclude" that General Jones's opinion on necessary and reasonable measures is a reasonable interpretation of the evidence. Now, first of all, it's, of course, for the Trial Chamber to determine whether, under the circumstances of the case, General Gotovina took necessary and reasonable measures. But to the extent an expert's views are relevant to that determination, it rests upon, among other things, the accuracy of that witness's underlying factual assumptions, since, of course, what constitutes necessary and reasonable measures depends on the circumstances of the particular case. And General Jones' conclusions were not based on accurate facts. They were based on significant misconceptions and uncertainties about the scope and nature of HV crime and the response to it. For example, the assumed facts that the Gotovina Defence provided to Jones made no mention of General Gotovina's subordinates committing any crimes before, during, or after Operation Storm. That's D1632. And in his report, General Jones still did not assume any facts involving HV crimes. He said: "I cannot refute that there was undisciplined behaviour in the area of operations," but stated that "whether this behaviour was conducted by soldiers, criminals, or refugees is not for me to determine." D1633, para 43. In court he first claimed to have knowledge of the extent of HV crimes prior to Storm, referring to the crimes in Grahovo as "isolated incidents," and then contradicting himself by stating: "I don't have the answer to the question, whether those were isolated or whether they were routine." T21040 to 41. And he disagreed with the proposition that General Gotovina's repeated orders regarding crime were ineffective based on his claim that: "Following this particular date you'll see an increase in the number of -- of arrests, investigations, and finding people culpable for all offences." His purported source was a Lausic report: "... stating the number of arrests, the number of convictions and what they have been able to accomplish based on all things that happened here to show control of the area and reinforcement of the rule of law." As we pointed out in our brief, there is no such report. That is found at paras 188 through 189. And we address General Jones's conclusions in more detail at paragraph 152, 163, and 188 through 191. So the problem with the Defence claim that "you must conclude that General Jones's opinion is a reasonable interpretation of the evidence" is that his opinions were not actually based on the evidence. The Defence has asserted in its submissions that: "The Prosecution also claims in its brief that there is no evidence of a single demobilised soldier subsequently being prosecuted for a crime." That's at paragraph 233. That's false. Or -- it's not correct. So see, for example, Your Honour, several of the examples contained within Exhibit D1381. Moreover the Defence said Witness Perkovic was a viva voce Defence witness who testified that he was demobilised while in custody as a result of his involvement allegedly for the Varivode murders, and was subsequently prosecuted for those murders. Now the Gotovina Defence has made two mischaracterisations here. First of all, the Prosecution did not claim that no demobilised soldier was ever subsequently prosecuted. At paragraph 233 of the Prosecution final brief, the point was made that the numbers of criminal proceedings for property destruction between the 4th and 17th August are negligible, and therefore that the "continuous" property destruction by the 134th Home Guard Brigade reported to the Split Military District on the 18th of August, crimes that the Defence claim were appropriately punished through the demobilisation of much of that unit, did not result in criminal sanctions, and none of the evidence cited by the Defence impacts that assertion. Beyond that, the Defence claim that Perkovic was "demobilised while in custody as a result of his involvement allegedly for the Varivode murders and subsequently prosecuted" suggests that Perkovic's demobilisation was part of his punishment. To the contrary, the evidence shows that Perkovic was demobilised and that his demobilisation date was falsified in order to conceal the fact that he was an HV member at the time of the crime. And that's in final brief footnote 304. Your Honours, yesterday you saw -- you heard some comments about Mr. Vanderostyne and a photograph. And the suggestion was that he'd said he was scared but was grinning, and that he was possibly colour-blind because he couldn't tell the uniforms of the special police from some other uniforms. Now first of all, Your Honours, you will recall that Mr. Vanderostyne was another of the internationals who witnessed the extensive and open destruction and crimes taking place and spoke about that quite forcefully. But in his statement he explained that there was no -- he was not confusing the uniforms of the special police. He distinguished those expressly from the uniforms of the regular police. And when he got into Gracac encountered the special police, and the Court had seen photographs of the special police looting openly in Gracac. And with respect to the photograph of Mr. Vanderostyne looking -- or with some kind of smile on his face, he talked about that. "We drove very slowly, not in aggressive mood and because it was a quite intense situation. Then we drove very slowly, windows open, nobody should feel threatened. And we parked the car and we tried to be relaxed, so in a more or less relaxed way we went to a little group of those soldiers that were drinking, that were relaxing under a tree." The effort to suggest to the Court that this witness was misleading the Court when he had, in fact, explained the very nature of the circumstances in which he found himself was unfair to that witness who -- whose testimony -- whose damning testimony could not be explained through some kind of attack on his bias because Mr. Vanderostyne was very explicit that he was someone who sympathised with the Croats because of their victimisation from the beginning part of the war. It was also significant to see those photographs to learn that Mr. Vanderostyne had interviewed the lieutenant involved in that, to see how openly it was done, to see a genuine manifestation of the climate of impunity. It was also asserted that Mr. Vanderostyne is the only witness upon whom the Court can find evidence related to Gracac and special police crimes in Gracac. The Court can look to the testimony of Mr. Steenbergen and also Annex A, pages 12 through 17. There was some attention paid yesterday to the Ramljane incident, and it was asserted by the Markac Defence that there's no evidence that General Markac knew where Grubori was or had any way -- or knew what was the Lucko Unit. No one identified the unit, nor is there any evidence that General Markac knew which unit went through Grubori on the evening of August 25th. I would direct the Court's attention to the following. You will recall, Your Honours, that before that search operation, the inner control branch based in Gracac would brief units and give each unit a package showing their precise axes of attack. And that included a map, indicating such. The Court has seen such a map, P559. In addition to the fact that inner control was there, the coordinator of the, operation Janic, was based in Gracac, was there on the evening of August 25th. And as I mentioned, inner control itself was there. All General Markac had to do, upon learning of the burnings, killings in Gracac was to pick up the phone, go down the road, and find out -- not in Gracac, excuse me, Your Honour, in Grubori and find out which unit was deployed in Grubori and ensure that that unit -- find out what had happened with that and ensure, if necessary, that that unit was not deployed to the next village which would be burned. The Court will recall the effort by the Markac Defence yesterday to focus on Mr. Celic because he implicates General Markac in the creation of false reports. And, in that respect, I simply want to turn the Court to the circumstances regarding the creation of that false report, P563, and I would turn the Court to paragraph 444 of the brief so as not to require going into private session and in particular see footnotes 1632. That evidence indicates that the report was written in Markac's immediate presence. Your Honour, I want to mention one matter that was raised yesterday. It's -- and that was the -- the restrictions of movement chart which the Court had asked about in question number 5. Prosecution noted that the focus of the submissions were largely on the footnoted materials relating to the date that the restrictions of movement existed. I would simply urge the Court to, in addition, look at footnote 1311. That's Annex A. Or directs the Court to Annex A, wanton destruction and plunder, to ensure that the Court is in a position to cross-reference the dates of restrictions of movement with the crimes that were taking place. Yesterday there was discussion by the Markac [sic] Defence concerning the awareness of what had happened in Grubori, what Mr. Dondo did -- knew and did, and the assertion that the entry in the Knin police log requesting an urgent sanitation of bodies should not be attributed to General Cermak. The suggestion was that the Prosecution was somehow artificially trying to upgrade General Cermak's involvement and move the Court away from the actual evidence. I would like to correct the transcript I said there was a discussion by the Markac Defence, that should have been the Cermak Defence. What the evidence indicates, Your Honour, is the following. That it was Dondo who requested an urgent clearing up of bodies. That's listed at P764 at page 2 -- excuse me, listed at D57, page 61, and in fact Dondo reported to Cermak at P764, page 2, that he made the report and he made such a request. Now, what the Court should also consider is the following. Of course, as we learned at T27883 through 27884, and as we know from other evidence, Mr. Dondo was General Cermak's subordinate, and both General Cermak and Mr. Dondo knew, when Dondo went to make that report, that the Knin police were already aware of the murders. Dondo tried to say that he only went down to report that the murders had taken place and that he hadn't ordered the sanitation and that -- had no idea how the entry in the log had taken place. But the Court will look at paragraph 438 of the Prosecution's brief and indeed paragraph 246 of the Cermak brief, you will see that Cermak, who hosted the dispute that existed about that issue regarding disposal, was aware of the -- aware that Knin police knew and Dondo knew; see his statement at D1695, paragraph 25. And as you'll see from the testimony, when you review it again, at 27883 and 27884, others concluded or were aware that Dondo had gone to the police station in the evening hours and there even said that sanitation must be carried out. There would have been no other reason for Dondo to go to the Knin police station other than for that purpose, because he and General Cermak were aware that they knew about the killings already. Your Honour, let me turn to the issue of meetings with President Tudjman by General Cermak. Mr. Kay said that there was no evidence regarding Mr. Cermak meeting with President Tudjman. That's at pages 78 through 79, so I would simply direct the Court's attention, in addition to the -- the obvious meeting on the 5th of August, meeting on the 6th of August in Knin; P2526, page 91; P2525, page 176. Cermak travelled to Zagreb to meet with the president; D1618, page 1. And General Cermak, of course, met with President Tudjman at the Freedom Train speech; P1144, P5, P473. Mr. Kay also discussed Exhibit P2527. That's the publication in which General Cervenko described General Cermak as President Tudjman's personal man of confidence. D1306 is the published retraction of that article in which Cervenko said it was unauthorised, accidental and disjointed, which was secretly recorded by the reporter. Mr. Kay suggested that the Prosecution failed to address that exhibit but, in fact, D1306 was cited in the Prosecution brief at footnote 892. Now yesterday Mr. Kay called the contents of that original article, which was recorded, gossip and of no real consequence. But it is noteworthy that the Cermak Defence cited the same exhibit in the Defence brief at -- in support of certain propositions it wanted to advance at paragraph 121. There was also discussion, Your Honours, about the Brioni meeting and the discussion concerning the role that -- that General Cermak assumed. And to demonstrate that there was no discussion at Brioni that touched upon General Cermak's ultimate responsibilities Mr. Kay said that he would read the exact text to the Court said: "The exact text is this." I'd like to actually look at that text, Your Honour, very quickly. What's in black is what was read by Mr. Kay. What's in red is what is in the transcript and what was not read. And what we see is that Minister Susak is referring to another staff and he had been talking before about a kind of staff for the immediate operation and then suggested: "We need another staff and that would be for relations with UNCRO, someone who would be a permanent liaison, someone who would be in touch with us and resolve things with them, for us to get instructions, because matters will evolve too rapidly for us to start looking around for them and calling them." So the minister of defence is talking about one person who is to be a permanent liaison for UNCRO on the ground. Unrelated to the issues that might arise during the operation itself. Now, on the heels of the psy-ops discussion, Minister Susak then raised the issue of setting up a propaganda staff which would be connected to the office of the president, and the head of that office was Mr. Sarinic. And you see that in this slide. That's at page 29, indicating: "We need someone -- would we need someone from your office in order to reestablish this staff for propaganda. We need someone from your office to be the contact person." And President Tudjman responded: "This is a question to be dealt with, what you just said, and also in reference to UNCRO, and that [sic] means Sarinic." So that was a matter to be dealt with. Sarinic was going to be the contact person, and it is therefore instructive that when Mr. Cermak -- or General Cermak, excuse me, was asked who was his immediate superior while he was in Knin, he answered: "My contacts with international organisations and delegations and so on, I had contacts with the office of the president, with Sarinic, with the president." And that's all consistent with General Cermak's description of himself as the "one contact person for the internationals." P2526 through 61 -- page 61. Everything came to him or went through him. P2525, page 12, and P2526, page 9. The Cermak Defence also suggested in its brief that the -- well, suggested to you during the submissions that Mr. Dzolic's evidence was a telling moment in the case and, in its brief, that the Prosecution had improperly put words in his mouth. That's found at 46 -- paragraphs 465 and 475. Mr. Dzolic, as you will recall, was the first commander of the Knin military police company. We would submit, Your Honour, that the telling moment in respect of Mr. Dzolic's evidence was when he was asked why the fact of his being called into Cermak's office on occasions would not be recorded in his log-book. And he explained why he was called in to General Cermak's office: "I was invited by General Cermak to come there for a conversation because I was subordinate to him in the daily tasks." So focussed on the issue of explaining why it wasn't in the log-book, he indicated in quick response what the reality was. Your Honours, the Cermak Defence also suggested that the Prosecution ignored evidence of General Cermak's experts and instead focussed primarily on issues of credibility during its cross-examination of those witnesses. Well, as the Court should recall, that's certainly not entirely correct. Recall, for example, Mr. Albiston who was cross-examined about the following. His testimony concerning General Cermak's authority and the revelation that he had failed to consider a key document that contradicted his opinion which demonstrated that civilian police carried out General Cermak's orders. And that's P510. That is an issue going very deeply to the substance of that witness's testimony. But to the extent that there was a focus on credibility during the course of those examinations, it was well founded and well directed. And I will direct the Court's attention to the testimony of Mr. Feldi, who did not disclose in his CV that he had been a member of the Markac Defence team, as well as a member of the Cermak Defence team before he wrote his report, and also failed to mention his involvement in and reliance upon the blue book which also came to light during his testimony. Your Honours, the Gotovina Defence claimed yesterday that because the Prosecution pleaded an armed conflict in the indictment, we are precluded from "relying upon an armed conflict which may be international in character," based upon their interpretation of the 21 February 2003 Hadzihasanovic Appeals Judgement. The Defence noted that there were no Article 2 charges in that case, and suggested that the Chamber's ruling was that the Prosecution is specifically required to plead an international armed conflict even where the character of the conflict is not relevant to the charges. That is not accurate. In the context of that decision, the 21 February 2003 Hadzihasanovic decision, prior to the subsequent clarification of the law, the character of the armed conflict was relevant because, at that time, it was unclear whether the legal rules underlying Article 3 applied in internal armed conflicts. Therefore, the absence of Article 2 charges did not render that a dead or meaningless issue, and there was still a question of whether or not the Prosecution needed to rely on the nature of the conflict as international in order for the charges to be valid. But in its 16 July 2003 decision, the Hadzihasanovic Appeals Chamber found that the Article 3 charges apply to both internal and international armed conflicts thereby rendering the pleading issue moot. And in this case too, Your Honour, the nature of the armed conflict is legally irrelevant. As we know from Article 5 charges, it's either an international or a non-international armed conflict. The same is true of the Article 3 charges in this case. They're grounded in customary international law which apply to all conflicts regardless of their classification. They simply require a nexus to an armed conflict. There is no requirement that that conflict be either international or non-international. We have pled and proved an armed conflict. And there was no requirement for the Prosecution to specifically plead the character of the armed conflict in this case. Irrelevant and pointless. Your Honours, I want to turn to one additional issue, and that's the argument by the Gotovina Defence that the Prosecution cannot decide whether General Gotovina was issuing effective or ineffective orders. Cannot keep its story straight, I think the language was. They referred several times to the political affairs attachment at D201, which states: "Familiarising units with a need to eliminate all negative occurrences that will surface in the course of combat operations with a focus on preventing torching and destruction of larger populated areas and towns." According to the Defence it is illogical for the Prosecution to argue that part of those "familiarising units with the need to eliminate all negative occurrences that will surface" was ineffective, while another part, "focus on preventing torching and destruction of larger populated areas and towns," was effective. Yet this distinction is quite clear and quite logical. What is illogical is the premise underlying the Defence argument that a commander's order can only be all effective or all ineffective. Whether a commander's orders are effective or not depends on the extent to which that commander ensures compliance with those orders. And, of course, he can choose to selectively enforce some orders while allowing others to be disobeyed. To go back to the example raised by General Gotovina Defence based on D201, let's recap the context. General Gotovina's subordinates were burning and looting in Operation Summer. The Split Military District Command ordered them to stop burning, they continued to burn, and they were not punished. This created a situation where yet another bald order not to burn, such as instruction in D201, would be ineffective. But the Gotovina Defence did not mention the instruction in P1126 to the OG commanders: "Prevent burning and looting of facilities in the liberated territory. Immediately station personnel of the MUP, special MUP units and military police in large towns to secure the town and important buildings." And here, Your Honours, he accompanied what would otherwise be a bald and, under the circumstances, ineffective instruction to prevent burning and looting with a concrete enforcement measure. And that is where the difference lies. Furthermore, the fact that General Gotovina felt the need to accompany a generic "don't loot and burn instruction," which the Defence says he intended to be effective, with a specific measure to protect certain facilities from his own subordinates indicates General Gotovina's awareness of the inadequacy of the generic measures under the circumstances. More generally, the Defence asks: "How a subordinate would know which are the orders which are supposed to be followed and which are the orders that are supposed to be ignored." The answer to that question is simple. A subordinate knows to follow an order when his superior monitors and enforces his subordinate's compliance and punishes or holds him accountable for failing to implement it. On the other hand, where the superior doesn't monitor the subordinate's implementation of the order, doesn't punish or hold the subordinate accountable for not implementing the order, and doesn't punish the underlying conduct when the disobedience involves criminal behaviour, when the commander repeats the same order, that is a signal to the subordinate that he need not follow the order. And the superior only strengthens that signal through additional repetitions of the same cycle of non-compliance and non-enforcement. Finally, Your Honour, we have referred throughout the submissions to the more detailed submissions in the Prosecution's final brief, per the Court's guidance. As the Court is aware, our sentencing submissions are found at paragraph 698 through 705. Those paragraphs detail relevant factors, including the scale of the crimes, the vulnerability of the victims and the impact on the victims. And in considering those factors, the Prosecution simply notes that particularly in considering impact, although it is often generic references to Krajina Serbs, these crimes were visited upon individuals and each person suffered individually. Your Honours, today's submissions, the submissions that preceded those to this Bench, the Prosecution's final brief, and the evidence adduced during the course of this case demonstrate beyond a reasonable doubt that General Gotovina, General Markac, and General Cermak are responsible under the law for those crimes. Your Honours, thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let me start off by addressing the point Mr. Tieger made concerning the phosphoric shells. Mr. President, I think the evidence is very clear, and we ask you to, first of all, look at the fact that the two opposing military commanders, General Gotovina and General Mladic, in both of their diaries, in one case a personal diary and in the other case the officially Military District diary, both on the same day make reference to HV use of incendiary munitions in the wider Grahovo-Glamoc area. The entry that Mr. Tieger referred to in the Split Military District diary is from the 2nd of August, which is, of course, the same day that it appears in Mladic's diary. I also would note that Mr. Tieger, while advancing an alternative argument, did not suggest that his argument or the argument of the Prosecution is the only reasonable interpretation of that evidence. And we suggest to you that any reasonable person looking at two entries on the same day by the opposing military commanders could, in fact, make a reasonable conclusion that phosphoric shells were being used in that area on that day or immediately prior to it. We would also note that to the extent the Prosecution alleges some sort of cover-up, we would ask the Chamber to consider, first, that prior to the 2nd of August, both the military police had been seized of the issue, and the minister of defence, in an entry on the 1st of August, the day before, had already been fully seized of the matter. So in terms of any allegation that General Gotovina was covering up within the Croatian system, it is unfounded. Moreover, saying that because General Gotovina didn't want media in Grahovo on the 2nd of August in light of the -- both the prior military conduct, which would include Operation Summer 95 but also the tactical operation of the ARSK which had taken place on the 1st of August and which is referenced in our brief, and in light of the fact that two days later, General Gotovina knew he would be launching Operation Storm, to not invite the media into the war zone is hardly a controversial decision by a military command. And indeed, I would argue it is a common-place decision in wars, particularly on the eve of combat. Turning next to the issue of General Jones. The bottom-line point here, Mr. President, is, it is absolutely clear in any fair reading of both his witness statement and his testimony, it is clear that he was aware of the allegation of crimes being committed in the Grahovo area and, in fact, he was specifically asked on direct examination whether General Gotovina took all necessary and reasonable measures in response to events in that operation and he testified that he did. So the suggestion that his -- that he lacked knowledge to form an opinion is unjustified. Moreover, it was never put to General Jones that he is -- whether his opinion would change if he were aware of certain information that the Prosecution had which the Prosecution believes might impact his opinion. It is expected when an expert is put on the stand and has an opinion that if the Prosecution or a party wishes to challenge the opinion, then other facts are put him and the expert is asked whether that would or would not change that opinion. That didn't happen here. And I would submit to you, Your Honours, that the Prosecution has taken the position that the measures that General Gotovina failed to take were "so obvious" that it's clear he didn't take necessary and reasonable measures. Well, if that is the case, why weren't these "so obvious" measures not only put to General Jones but, I repeat, many, if not most of them -- I should say, most of them were never put to anyone. Why wasn't General Jones asked whether, for example, he would have imposed a military curfew in Croatia. And I would add that to the extent that the Prosecution is now arguing that the military curfew should have only applied to the military, the -- the terminology then is not being used properly as to what a military curfew really means. With respect to the issue of demobilisation, there is an allegation that Mr. Perkovic was demobilised in order to cover up HV involvement. That is not something that Prosecutor Galovic agreed with. This is -- he testified on this point and it's transcript 19812, beginning at line 14. Moreover, what is ignored is that, in fact, Mr. Perkovic was prosecuted for the crime. So it is difficult to see what it is exactly that was not done in terms of punishing or trying to punish the perpetrators in the Varivode murders. I would also asking on this point the Trial Chamber to keep in mind that in Exhibit 2614, there were 120 cases of criminal charges against members of the Split Military District for crimes committed in the liberated territory and it was 120 cases for murder and looting. Finally, Mr. President, Exhibit D201. I must confess that I am pleased that I think we've come to some sort of inadvertent agreement. We've now pushed the issue far enough that we not only have the Prosecution conceding that General Gotovina issued orders to prevent burning and looting and other crimes. We now have a concession from the Prosecution that General Gotovina took steps to make sure at least one of those orders was implemented. We have common ground here now. Now, let us take a look at P1126, which Mr. Tieger relied on this morning. And this is page 3. Let's see what the measure was. "Prevent burning and looting of facilities in the liberated territory. Immediately station personnel of the MUP, special MUP units and military police in large towns to secure the town and important buildings." Your Honours, first of all, our position is that what General Gotovina was doing here was implementing the agreement that had been reached between the minister of the interior and minister of defence as to who was going to be responsible for security in the liberated area. Second, I believe there is no dispute, and it will be an uncontested fact, that General Gotovina had no command over the MUP and no command over the special MUP units. What does this mean? The Prosecution says that General Gotovina implemented his orders by relying on the other institutions of the Republic of Croatia, including MUP, including special MUP units and the military police, and that that made his order effective. Now, we're not going to relitigate the issue of who had the responsibility to continue to deploy the military police after Operation Storm commenced. You will make that decision, and you know our position on it very well. If you agree with us, that it was Mr. Lausic and Mr. Juric who were responsible for implementing that portion, then what we have this morning is the Prosecution saying, When General Gotovina issues an order and relies on the MUP and the military police, he should know that his order is going to be effective. We ask to you keep that in mind. And how many other orders General Gotovina could have issued relying on the MUP and the military police and the political affairs branch and the SIS to make sure that those orders get implemented. Finally, Mr. President, we note that D204 was not addressed and we -- with respect to General Gotovina taking measures. As Mr. Tieger said, he took measures. It was not only to rely on the MUP, the special MUP units, the military police, SIS, Political affairs, he also issued D204 for disciplinary measures, P918, and we know that the result was a 151 per cent increase in disciplinary measures in the Split Military District. Mr. President, Your Honour, I thank you very much for listening to me today and for two and a half years, and I thank you, and I cede the floor to Mr. Kehoe.
