utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Once again in rebuttal argument by the Prosecution, we have observed their use of this evidence to try to demonstrate the illegal intent of General Gotovina. Yet in this task, they once again, as they have done continuously, overlook what they describe as the context of everything that happened. And we're not go to, at this juncture, Mr. President, rehash the context of all of these items. But just a couple of salient features and questions to be asked when the Chamber is reviewing the rebuttal argument by Mr. Tieger directed to the intent of General Gotovina. His argument was that the activities of General Gotovina and the HV were unlawful, along with the other alleged JCE members, because they intended to drive the civilian population out of the so-called Krajina, with most of the emphasis by the Prosecution on Knin. Well, the questions to be asked that haven't been addressed by the Prosecution that play into that are twofold. If not only officials within the Croatian government but others, such as Ambassador Galbraith and Ambassador Holbrooke, believed that no more than 20 per cent of the Serbs would come back under any circumstances, why would this large entity within the government risk losing relations or damaging relations with the United States and other legal entities and countries throughout the Western world? Taking it down to the more specific, the position of the Prosecution once again this morning is that after the Brioni meeting, the artillery attack that was directed by General Gotovina was to force the civilian population out of Knin. If that were the case, and this wasn't a classic military offensive, as has been demonstrated by the evidence put forth by the Defence, if that were the case, and the point was to scare the civilian population and drive them out, why not just line up, after the fall of Grahovo and Glamoc, and shell Knin? Your Honour, Judge Orie, I know that you are quite familiar with the facts in Sarajevo and certainly don't stand here to duplicate that. Nevertheless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, apart from that, Mr. Kehoe. I'm not going to rely on whatever I learned in the past about Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because it is not part -- to the extent it is not part of the evidence in this case. Let that be perfectly clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I understand, Mr. President. The fact of the matter is, if you want to terrorise the civilian population, you do what the Serbs did in Sarajevo and shell intermittently three or four shells, how about on the 28th of July, the 29th of July, the 30th, the 1st, 2nd and 3rd of August. That would terrorise the civilian population and drive them out. That didn't happen. And certainly Your Honours are aware that they had more than the capability to do it. Secondly, if the shelling of Knin was so concentrated in civilian areas on the 4th of August, why was the civilian population leaving front line areas to go to Knin? Next question. In going into the intent of the JCE, and the intent being that this JCE was going to allow crimes to take place, that they wanted those crimes to take place, because it was part and parcel of this artillery plan to drive the Serbs out. Really? Why did the Prosecution not address the fact that there were numerous meetings, both before Operation Storm and throughout August of which we have numerous documents to evidence, numerous meetings where the discussion was, How do we prevent crime and how do we do a better job? None of which, I might add, was attended by General Gotovina. Let us move to the artillery issue as argued by Mr. Tieger this morning. A thousand shells fell on Knin, per Mr. Tieger. 900 shells, Mr. Tieger noted for us, were actually on civilians. There's absolutely no evidence whatsoever of 900 shells falling on civilians. Nine-tenths of the shells fired into Knin were allegedly -- without any evidence and without any foundation from the Prosecution, they maintain fell on -- on the civilians. Where is the evidence of that in the record? They gave us a 300-page brief. We are now on our third day of final arguments and there is no evidence to support that. And assuming, assuming for the sake of argument that that was the case. Why would Steiner Hjertnes go back and report, in his provisional report and his final report, which I add was verified by Mr. Roberts, why did he tell this Chamber that the shelling was concentrated on military targets? Which, by the way, is consistent the ARSK intelligence report in D389 which was a contemporaneous record demonstrating the same thing. But why is that discussion -- question never answered, that given these -- and I say outlandish, and I don't mean to say that lightly but that's exactly what it is. This outlandish allegation that 900 shells fell on civilians, that that fact was lost on experienced military officers, as well as the media, as well as the international community, when they came to visit Knin after the 5th of August. Even Forand, General Forand, when he gave his first speech on this in 1996, noted that the use of artillery was excellent. It was only until that statement, that speech was put in the hands of Mr. Robertson that things changed. Let's take a look at exactly what he said. This is P339, page 4. Excuse me, D339 page 4. Now I note for Your Honour, I know it's been some time since this was actually looked upon or viewed. It notes and I add -- I note for you just to reference you back, is the stuff in blue underline is the information that was inserted after this statement or speech was gotten -- was in the hands of Mr. Robertsson. But initially, he noted that: "Their," being the HV, "use of artillery was excellent." He noted that there were problems with the tanks and infantry, but I note, the use of the artillery was excellent. Why was that so dramatically, dramatically changed by Mr. Robertson? And why has there never been any explanation by the Prosecution for this? Let us turn to the discussion of craters and the evidence of craters, because, of course, crater analysis has been used not only by military but, of course, by courts to demonstrate any number of things. Nevertheless, today, Mr. Tieger noted at page 10, line 18: "Crater analyses are intended to determine the origin of -- of -- for the use in situations in which it is not clear which warring faction is responsible for firing the projectile." That's true. That is one of the reasons. It's also preliminarily used to demonstrate that shelling actually took place. The reason we look for crater analyses at various locations evidentiary-wise is to show that it took place and how many shells were actually shot at a particular target or an area. Moreover, those shelling analyses, the crater analysis is also done to determine what the munition is, what type of cannon, what type of gun, what type of piece of artillery fired this. And, of course, where was it located. None of those items, none of those pieces of evidence, those crucial pieces of evidence to substantiate an illegal attack on the civilian population has been presented to this Chamber, barring one crater analysis by Mr. Munkelien and Mr. Anttila, and when you go back to the record, they have three different locations for where the actual rocket was found. There's one in the report, there's one in the testimony of Mr. Munkelien and one in the testimony of Mr. Anttila. All three are different. They can't even agree. And that is even before we engage in a discussion as to what type of munition this was and who fired it. The principle of distinction. Mr. Tieger noted that General Gotovina violated the principle of distinction by the use of the weaponry employed and deployed during Operation Storm. Well, that's interesting, Mr. President, and we discuss that in our brief, but I asked that question of Colonel Konings, specifically directed on the use of -- on the principle of distinction and the use of MRLs and cannons as well as T130s. And he -- I asked him, Can this weaponry be used to hit this target, a target? He said yes. He confirmed, as we outline in our brief, that he -- the violation -- that the principle of distinction was not violated by the use of MRLs and other pieces of artillery. Suffice it to say, the OTP never addresses, never addresses, the consistent and sophisticated use of artillery both at the point of contact on front lines as well as in depth. Nor have they contested the fact that it worked. In their zeal to try to prove that this was an attack against the civilian population, they overlook a very crucial issue: That the purpose of this artillery, among other things, was to comprise the three C/I capabilities of the ARSK; command, control, communication, and intelligence. And the evidence that's before this Chamber directly from General Mrksic was that it worked. His ability to communicate with the front lines on the Drina on the 4th, compromised. His ability to talk his troops in the Velebit, compromised. All as a result of the use of artillery which led to the decision that to avoid encirclement to evacuate the area. So, if the OTP's analysis is to be true -- is to followed, this was simply an illegal attack on the civilian population, which, by the way, happened to compromise the intelligence and communication capabilities of the ARSK headquarters, and that was just an ancillary benefit. That is a specious argument that there is no basis in reality and no basis in the evidence of this record. Lastly, this argument with regard to what General Gotovina should have done. Both my colleagues addressed this at some point concerning Jajce, and I don't quite know if they don't understand what a military curfew is or have overlooked that but a military curfew is not just a curfew against military, Mr. President, Your Honours. When you employ a military curfew in occupied territory, that means everybody is under curfew. Everybody in the occupied territory is under the curfew. Something that General Gotovina could not do given the fact that after the 6th of August, the constitutional order of Croatia was restored and civilian authorities took over. Nevertheless, as just mentioned by my colleague Mr. Misetic, General Gotovina took steps to implement as best he could those measures of controlling his troops by ordering on the 10th of August, in D204, as mentioned by Mr. Misetic, that arbitrary movement of troops should stop and be avoided, and to take resolute measures against anybody who conducts himself in an undisciplined manner. Mr. President, in conclusion, General Gotovina is not going to speak to the Chamber. He -- we will speak on his behalf. I think what we see through the evidence in all this and I submit to the Chamber is a soldier, a patriot, who acted honourably under very difficult circumstances with an attempt to do the right thing, to restore democracy to his country by the use of the military and the soldiers under his command. These were very difficult times, as this Chamber knows. The war in the former Yugoslavia raged between 1991 and 1995, and many, many difficult problems came before those involved in that endeavour that have now been sent to this Court to be revisited and discussed. But I submit to Your Honours that when the Chamber reviews the evidence in this case and the conduct of General Gotovina throughout, the Chamber will found that conduct to be both honourable, correct and right. We understand these are difficult issues. We have been here two and a half years. We understand that the Chamber has many, many questions to be answered over the months that it takes to render this decision. But we submit to the Chamber that when Your Honours reviews this evidence, you will find that not only General Gotovina acted in the right but so was the Defence that was presented to this Chamber. In history we're all -- have experience with difficult times. Of course, we look back at this difficult time in Croatia and in the former Yugoslavia. But I go back to the history in my country and we had our difficult times, and certainly the worse time was the American Civil War, where any number of individuals were killed, 650.000, to be exact. And somehow throughout all this, right and the truth willed out under those very difficult circumstances. And on the eve of that war, the horrible, horrible war, Abraham Lincoln stood at the Cooper Union in February of 1860, and he spoke these words: "And so let us have faith that right makes might, and in that faith, let us, to the end, dare to do our duty as we understand it." This is a difficult case. We submit to the Chamber, at this point, on behalf of General Gotovina, is that the right thing is to find General Gotovina not guilty of these charges and send him home to his family. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. I'll a bit puzzled by one of your lines. That is that you submit to the Chamber when we review the evidence that we will find that not only General Gotovina acted in the right, I take it that our verdict will give an answer to that question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but so was the Defence that was presented to this Chamber. I -- are you expecting us to include in the judgement --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- apart from what --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether Mr. Gotovina was right or wrong, whether your Defence was right or wrong ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, what we have tried to do throughout all this was just to give you what you needed to make this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your Defence you have drawn our attention to everything which you say demonstrates that General Gotovina did the right thing. That's what you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then I have understood you well, a bit perhaps beyond to what you literally said. Mr. Kay, are you next in line?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will address the issues raised by Mr. Tieger today. And, first of all, the first place to start is the issue of the Brioni meeting. Paragraph 347 in the Prosecution final brief where they clearly state that there was an envisaged role, and a planned role, for the person who eventually went to Knin in relation to tasks to be performed and that, ultimately, Mr. Cermak was chosen. This requires us, I believe, to go carefully to that exhibit, P461, consider the language now, because we say this clearly is not the case, that at the alleged JCE meeting, Mr. Cermak's role was envisaged. Page 27 of P461. They are talking about the planned combat operation. Susak says: "I'm talking about is when they start shelling. We might have up to 100.000 refugees. Panic might arise. They might shell him so heavily that a stampede might occur overnight." And goes on to say: "We must be organised in such a manner so as not to provoke panic here. Otherwise, they will have achieved a countereffect." And the president talks about stopping them at Dakovici. Susak says: "Second, we must give clear instructions to the commanders on the ground, Mr. President, about how to react if UNCRO becomes involved." And refers to the Canadians: "We must give them clear instructions. That's one thing. Second, I was thinking, Mr. President, that would be one staff." So one staff, the commanders on the ground, reacting to what was happening and dealing with UNCRO, plainly applies to the combat. "Another staff would be for relations with UNCRO. Someone who would be a permanent liaison. Someone who would be in touch with us and resolve things with them. For us to get instructions because matters will evolve too rapidly for us to start looking around for them and calling them. That's the second problem, as I see it." It's another member of staff for the combat operation. They go on to discuss matters. The Court will see that. Page 28, they discuss the operation. Page 29: "Can we have your agreement provided that we will face risks if we lose." That's what Susak said. No certain outcome for them in Brioni that they were going to win this war, this battle. They go on to talk about it, the need for leaflets, the need to try and present their operation as being a victory. Let go to where Susak speaks again. Number 3: "Another matter, Mr. President. In that case, would we not need someone from your office, in order to re-establish the staff for propaganda? We established this staff in Posusje but now this is being returned to Zagreb today. We need someone from your office to be the contact person." President Tudjman says: "This is a question to be dealt with." And that's to do with the propaganda leaflets. "With what you just said and also in reference to UNCRO," and that refers to the UNCRO reference on page 27. "And this means Sarinic. What I'd like to know is whether it is safer to coordinate and manage affairs from Brioni or Zagreb." And the advice was given by Susak that it would be better to coordinate in Zagreb. "It would be bad to coordinate from here," meaning Brioni. And that decision was made as we know. On page 30, the matter is further discussed concerning the operation. Page 31, Susak: "And, last, Mr. President, if it were Sarinic who's already in contact with the main commander here, they would each, at their own level, have to establish some kind of contact to tell the ones over here how far ahead they should give it." There is an interjection from Mr. Markac: "They didn't want to give it on time. This time we should just give them an hour, just enough to take cover." And that refers to giving notice to the international organisations concerning notice of the attacked, and Sarinic was to establish, through his contact at his level, and pass on that information. There it is in full. In our submission, it quite clearly does not refer to Mr. Cermak's role in post-Operation Oluja in Knin. He was never envisaged in Brioni, and a role was not carved out for him, as is attempted to be alleged, to take part in the alleged JCE. Moving on now to a further issue that arose concerning Grubori. Mr. Tieger referred to the false reports and the special police this morning and referred to Witness Celic. We want to stress one matter, first of all. It's clear through P607, Exhibit P607, that on the 25th of August, the Split special police unit had reported to Janic and filed a report, certainly by 4.00, which was sent to Zeljko Sacic, concerning the finding of a body in Vundici village, near the little bridge by the main road. The deceased had military boots, and his hands were tied. "I reported hourly to Mr. Janic on my position. There were no injured workers in the task." And that was sent on the 25th of August, a special police operations team with 102 people involved, hourly in contact with Janic, who we know went back to Gracac and he was in possession of that information. The special police at Gracac, on that 25th of August, had the information they needed to supply Cermak with a false story which he gave on the morning of the 26th of August, giving what he had been told by them to the UNTV. An important document in relation to a sequence of difficult documents as to who wrote what, when. But the time a document arises is not necessarily the time of the conception of the deceit within the document. That is something we stress. Documents may arise later, after the conception of the deceit. Just moving on to issues raised concerning Mr. Dondo's report. Mr. Dondo reported to the police five killings had taken place. That we know. It is D57 which is the record that states that the sanitation had been ordered. That is to civilian protection from the local police. There are distinct lines of hierarchy here, and from what we know of the Croatian system, that is certainly not something that Dondo, a Croatian army liaison officer, had any power or authority to order to the MUP. We do know, however, that the villagers in Grubori were concerned about the dead bodies and concerned about the effect it was having. On the 25th of August, P874, one of the Grubori villagers said to the journalist: "What am I to do now? Are you going to bury him? Who is going to bury him, my husband? We don't have anybody to do the burial." Dondo mentioning the need for sanitation was clearly in response to the attitude and position of the villagers. Transcript page 22593. P237, Mr. Romassev's note, the chief of the UNCIVPOL. He was aware that the villagers wanted the bodies buried. Linking the sanitation or the burial of the bodies with an attempt to thwart an investigation, in our submission, is taking a far more complicated and wrong position on this evidence. Not only that; we know that when Dondo went to the police, Mr. Cermak had not been involved with this matter since earlier in the afternoon, when the president came to Knin, and he went off to Split. To suggest that he'd ordered anything of Dondo is completely wrong. Dondo didn't know he was going to find five bodies when he went up there. The MUP report at 3.00 in D57, is of the two bodies. Let us consider, then, the position of Dondo in the report that he wrote; Exhibit P764, referred to by Mr. Tieger. The line he writes is: "Most probably the bodies will be cleared up on the 27th of August." Not "will be," not as a result of an order. But just passing on a factual answer of "most probably." And we know that on the 26th of August, the on-site investigation had been booked. That was in the police log in Knin. And we know that the entries for the civilian protection to also attend are part of a conjoined procedure for dealing with deaths, as is usual within the Croatian system. I only have a few minutes now. The issue concerning Mr. Albiston re the document 510, the Trial Chamber is invited to completely consider all the transcript on this matter. Because, first of all, the document that was produced was not a correct translation when questioned by the Prosecutor, and we can see that at 23957. And what the expert witness Albiston said was that he had considered this document. He had seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: (redacted) And on the totality of the document that he was considering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I've just realised, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Back in public session now, Your Honour, and I'm just making a closing remark. That passage of transcript that I've just read from Mr. Albiston, a police officer of great experience, like General Sir Jack Deverell, an army officer of great experience, in our submission, brings to bear some common sense in relation to the facts in this case. Our submission is that Mr. Cermak was a man put into Knin with a distinct mission which he tried to fulfil without any criminal intent or motivation in his mind. A position that was not well thought out, that was not clearly defined, but he attempted to do his best. Our submission is the verdict of this Court on all counts in relation to him should be one of not guilty. And we thank the Court for hearing us during this trial, and our colleagues from all parts of the courtroom, Prosecution, fellow Defence counsel, and those who have helped in the background during the course of this trial. And we leave the verdict to be announced in the hands of Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Mikulicic, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. Thank you. [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will very briefly dwell upon two issues raised by the Prosecution. It is about the alleged provocation that was carried out just before Operation Storm and which was discussed on the 31st of July in Brioni. I'm referring to P614. The Defence certainly does not say that initiating certain activities as a precondition for launching Operation Storm that certain -- doesn't say that these things were not discussed. But the OTP is going one step further and claims that based on P831, this provocation was, indeed, carried out and that my client, General Markac, took part in that. The Defence denies such an interpretation of P831 and claims that there has been no provocation either by General Markac or by anybody else, and would like to point out that this exhibit does not lend itself to such interpretation. In paragraph 3(C) of the ECMM says that Gospic was shelled. And I will continue in English. [In English] The UN and UNMOs believe the explosions heard may have been caused by the HV. [Interpretation] Finally there is a comment which says: [In English] Indeed, why should I, at the present moment. [Interpretation] If a sensible observer wants to interpret that document, he or she will arrive at the conclusion that this is speculation and that there is no reliable evidence showing, A, that there were indeed explosions; B, what the -- the intensity, the qualification and the location of those explosions were; and C, what the cause of these explosions was. Linking this to considerations raised at a meeting actually is speculation in the interpretation of the evidence which the Defence naturally opposes. Mr. Kuzmanovic had earlier spoken about the importance of the creation of certain preconditions and about the tactics employed in that military operation, but that is something that I don't want to go into. I do want to say, though, that a conversation and considerations about some military activities that did not happen cannot be incriminated because that would be a thought crime. Another issue is the testimony of Mr. Vanderostyne and based on his testimony the OTP bases the conclusion that it has been proven that the members of the special police looted the abandoned property of the Krajina Serbs. First of all, the OTP relies on P324 in reaching this conclusion. I will add that these are photographs taken on the 8th of August, 1995, on the streets of Gracac. The Defence submits that Witness Vanderostyne is unreliable in his memory and his interpretation of the events and that, therefore, his words are not a reliable basis for approving some facts. I would like to say that Mr. Vanderostyne, having arrived in Zagreb on the 5th of August, 1995, and having travelled to Gracac, passed through the Croatian towns of Karlovac and Otocac of which he said that they were considerably damaged due to shelling and that the population was -- was upset. But he fails to say that these are towns that for four years had been shelled by the forces of the so-called Army of the Serbian Krajina. So Mr. Vanderostyne is unaware of the context as well as the political and factual situation in which he was. The contentious photograph, which you will remember, showing a person putting on or taking off a truck a rectangular object is the basis -- is taken as evidence by the OTP that members of the special police stole things. Mr. Vanderostyne, in his statement, said that he noticed uniformed persons stealing property from houses, and he describes the uniforms as grey, greyish blue or khaki, respectively. The Chamber is aware that the special police didn't wear such uniforms, and evidence has been led to show that. That photograph does show a member of the special police wearing his standard green uniform. However, Ms. Mahindaratne, when she was examining the witness, was the one who suggested to him, who put to him, that the object in the photograph was actually a TV set. Witness Vanderostyne never said himself or never volunteered the opinion that it might be a TV set. I refer to transcript page 4028, line 23. After some time in the continued examination, Witness Vanderostyne said that he personally never saw the scene which was photographed, that the photograph was taken by his photographer, and that, at the time, he was not with the photographer. Your Honours, what is the value of his testimony? An interpretation of a photograph that anybody here can interpret because he was not personally present, nor did he see the context in which the photograph was taken. So that his interpretation, which, by the way, was put it him by the OTP, saying that it was a TV set is one possible interpretation only. To the question of the Defence whether in that particular case that may have been a cardboard box for documents or anything of that kind, the OTP protested and said that it was a fact to be established by the Trial Chamber. I agree with that, Your Honours. Let the Trial Chamber, by looking at the photograph, draw the conclusion whether it is, indeed, evidence of special police looting, or whether another conclusion can be drawn from that in accordance with the submission of the Defence, such as the removal of the staff of the special police from Gracac and the loading of equipment and materiel. Your Honours, by way of conclusion at the end of this lengthy procedure, I wish to thank you, first of all, as well as all representatives of this Tribunal who assisted in the trial, by which I mean Registry staff and the interpreters as well as court reporters. I would like to thank you for your patience and for your -- for your listening to us. And all our argumentation boils down to something very simple, that our client was an honourable person who devoted the best years of his life to one goal: The defence of his country and the defence of the democratic system of that country, the Republic of Croatia, in the very harsh conditions of Mount Velebit. I'm sorry that we were unable to go there so that the Trial Chamber see for themselves what it's like there. That it's a person -- we're talking about a person who carried out his duties honourably and honestly, who led highly trained professionals in the special police who went about their job in accordance with their ethics and their convictions. I don't believe that my client ever acted dishonourably, let alone in a way that can be characterised as committing a crime. Hence, I claim that the OTP has not led any evidence based on which the Trial Chamber can convict my client. As I said yesterday, that is the absence of legal prerequisites for convicting my client. It is the position of the Markac Defence that the only possible decision that can be taken by the Trial Chamber after duly considering all facts will be the acquittal of General Markac. And that will be a satisfactory outcome which will return General Markac to his family and friends in Zagreb, although in spite of the great sacrifice he has made. Thank you very much once again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. There are three areas I'm going to cover. The first deals with Mr. Celic; the second deals with Ramljane; and the third deals with Gracac. Mr. Tieger in his rebuttal argument discussed paragraph 444 of the Prosecution brief by telling you that the second report relating to Grubori, P576, actually it wasn't relating to Grubori, it was relating to the Plavno mop-up operation, was written in Markac's presence. But not even Mr. Celic says that. The report at issue is alleged to have been dictated to Celic by Sacic at Gracac HQ outside of Markac's presence. The information, as I talked about yesterday, that are in the reports of General Markac are all information that he receives from subordinates, and in the case of Grubori, it's misinformation. And all of this misinformation starts with Celic. Markac isn't present in Grubori. He's provided information by his subordinates regarding this mop-up operation, and what's interesting is that, as I described yesterday, Mr. Celic has somewhat of an uncanny ability to agree with everyone. He agrees that nothing happened. Then when he's confronted in cross-examination or by questions from the Bench about the alleged role of Sacic and Sacic dictating to him what happened, and whether or not he believed what Sacic was telling him was the truth, he says, Absolutely. Again, when Josip Turkalj, on September 1st, after General Markac requests reports, orders a report from the group leaders, what happens? Again, the same thing. Misinformation. Not just from the group leaders but again from Celic. What evidence is there that General Markac ever influenced or obstructed information relating to Grubori? None. Zeljko Zganjer testified to that effect, the state prosecutor, who investigated this in 2001. Now -- and we need to go into private session for this, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, counsel. I just need to indicate that we are now in open session. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you thanked for that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for that. Thank you. I would now like to move to the discussion on Ramljane. Again, unlike the event in Grubori the day before, Markac did arrive in Ramljane. And yesterday I cited from Janic's testimony that he, as the responsible commander, looked into Ramljane and decided that there was no need to conduct any kind of disciplinary measures. What I did not include and what I will include out of Janic 's testimony at 6193, beginning at line 23 to 6194, and he's talking about Ramljane. And Janic says: "Later on before departure or before we went other own separate ways, the general," referring to General Markac, "trusted me with verifying all this information and to interview the commander of Lucko and other commanders in order to verify whether the reports were true. After these interviews, I established that this is exactly what happened." Now it's the Office of the Prosecutor's position that the inner control now of the special police was somehow the source for Markac to know at 5.00 on August 25th that out of the six special police units of 580 members, it was Lucko that was in Grubori, and because of that, he shouldn't have sent Lucko into Ramljane. Well, I didn't -- I believe I adequately explained yesterday how that was not possible under the evidence that's been admitted in this case. There's no evidence where General Markac was on August 25th, was he in Gracac, was he elsewhere? Now there is no reason for him to call Sacic to go down there if he already knows that it's the Lucko Unit -- if he has all the information by 5.00 on August 25th, what reason is there for him to ask Sacic to go down and find out what happened, as Sacic said. And we still -- the Prosecution has still not demonstrated beyond a reasonable doubt that Markac knew Lucko was in Grubori before the Ramljane Freedom Train operation. Let's talk about Gracac for a moment. Mr. Russo yesterday said -- or two days ago said that the Janic reference he provided discussed Gracac and targets in Gracac. Well, that's not what it discussed. I showed you the transcript that he referred to. Now they bring us to another transcript, and says, well, yes, Janic does refer to Gracac and targeting and targets. Well, that reference is page 6355 to 56. And when we go to that reference, at line 19, Mr. Janic is asked: "To the best of your recollection of the days spent in Gracac, can you tell us what the situation in town -- what was the situation in town? Were there -- was there any damage on the buildings? Just in a couple of sentences. "A. Since after I reached the road near Prezid, I entered Gracac and I can confirm that the town was intact. There was no damage caused by artillery. There was no immediate fighting over this particular town. Therefore, that there was no reason, and I know that near the town there were some military depots that were legitimate targets. But the town itself wasn't. And there was no fighting inside it. And there were no artillery strikes targeting the town." Mr. Janic doesn't talk about military targets in the town. He says the town itself wasn't targeted. There's a big difference. The Prosecution is very critical of various orders saying put certain towns under fire. Well, here's Mr. Janic saying, There were no artillery strikes targeting the town. Of course, the Prosecution has conveniently ignored the citations to Turkalj yesterday that I made and the other witnesses that I identified, and I will not go over them. However, I will refer to Mr. Vurnek, his testimony at 26257, asking him: "Did you see any craters from shelling in various parts all over the town, as Mr. Steenbergen says in his statement? "A. No. I saw several craters at the cross-roads just outside the town. As for the town itself, I don't recall there being any." The Court will recall that Mr. Vurnek was a witness of the Defence from the special police. Mr. Vitez, similarly a Defence witness, from 25988 through 25989, talks about damage. But he says: "In Gracac, as far as I remember, they had been destroyed a long time previously. There had been vegetation growing out of the ruins. I don't remember any other damage. Witness Cvrk also describes, 25375 through 25376. Witness Turkalj, in a reference that I didn't make yesterday, states at 13772: "I was surprised at that fact at that there was no civilian population there," and he is referring to Gracac. "It was already said that the targets engaged in Gracac were engaged with an exceptionally small number were projectiles, in view of the number of targets in Gracac. To draw a comparison, I was present in the area of the town of Karlovac, where hundreds or even thousands of rounds landed on Karlovac and the population never abandoned it. It was always there. So the movements of the population can never be correlated with the activities of shelling. Or at least I could not when it came to the shelling of towns that came from our side." Witness Herman, also a Defence witness, transcript reference 26435 through 26436, describes, apart from some craters that could be seen on the tarmac, he talked about the main road in Gracac. It was in fair condition. So as far as the citation references regarding Gracac, they're either non-existent or completely misinterpreted. The last thing I wanted to state, Your Honour, in conjunction with my colleague Mr. Mikulicic is, while I thanked many people yesterday I didn't thank the three of you, Judges, for listening to us, for your patience, for your obvious engagement in the case, and for at times knowing certain portions of the case better than the Defence lawyers or the Prosecution. I join my colleague Mr. Mikulicic in seeking our client's acquittal because the Prosecution has not proven its case beyond a reasonable doubt. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before you conclude, one small housekeeping matter. I just wanted to indicate in keeping with what we have done thus far, should the Court wish the Prosecution to provide the slides shown today we're prepared to do so but leave it to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's resolve this in the following manner. If any of the parties would like to receive it, they will address you, Mr. Tieger, and once you send a hard copy or an electronic copy to any of the Defence teams, the Chamber would like to receive a similar copy. We're not yet at the end. I just want to have a few matters clear for myself. Mr. Akhavan, you've more or less assumed that silence would be understood as -- as an expression of a position. Did I miss something, and that is very well possible, that you did not explicitly respond on the Hadzihasanovic argument raised by Mr. Tieger, that where the character of the conflict may have been of some importance in the Hadzihasanovic case that it does not anymore, is that a matter which you would like to further address?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll understand that I was hesitant to consider it to be -- having acceded to the position of the Prosecution. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. First of all, the Hadzihasanovic case did not deal with the scope of application of international versus international armed conflict, a matter which, as you appreciate, was resolved in a Tadic jurisdiction decision quite some earlier. It dealt with the allegation that Article 7(3) does not apply in internal armed conflict. But the point from that decision is that the Trial -- the Appeals Chamber clearly stipulates that in order to rely on international armed conflict, it must be expressly charged in the indictment, and to the extent that the Prosecution is relying on an international armed conflict to vest this Court with jurisdiction, it must have expressly stipulated that in the indictment. That is the issue. And I would add also that the Dragomir Milosevic case in 2005, I believe, had a similar finding as Hadzihasanovic. Unfortunately, I haven't had time to find that precedent for you. So we do not concede the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. I took it from Mr. Tieger's position that he doesn't not rely on anything you say he should then present or put to the Chamber. But that's at least clarified. I have one also for you, a small question. You pointed at the Eritrea-Ethiopia Claims Commission. Would you agree with me that the way in which you presented that was more or less a one-liner. You see how broad the powers are of a belligerent state to expel a mass expulsion of enemy aliens. You relied on Lauterpacht, the 1996 edition. Would you agree with me that that matter is far more complex as explained by the study of the ILC in 2006, and that have to fully appreciate the matters that apart from your one-liner pointing at the broad -- the broad powers that for a Chamber to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please switch off all unnecessary microphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My microphone is on necessarily at this moment. Would you agree with me for a Chamber to have a broader and a more balanced view on the matter that it should consider these elements as well, and would you consider that to be appropriate in dealing with the matter, which, by the way, was only a subsidiary argument for you because you said we would -- Croatia would have had those powers, although that was not the reason why the Serbs left the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We did not invoke that authority to justify a nonexistent mass expulsion, as I tried to explain. The point is that it is permissible for a state to deny the mass return of enemy aliens in armed conflict, and that the issue here, that the Prosecution is relying on a policy of no immediate mass return in order to infer criminal intention, and we believe that is inappropriate. The International Law Commission study that you refer to, of course, is relevant and there was also a study prepared by the secretariat prior to that which was submitted to the International Law Commission. I referred briefly in my presentation to the fact that in the cases of state succession, which is what we have before us, the customary rule arguably is that habitual residents of the new successor state must have the right to citizenship of that state, at least where they become stateless. Now, in this case, you have an armed rebellion against a state and those who are supporting the armed rebellion are in effect citizens of the predecessor state, the SFRY. And in that context, none of them had Croatian citizenship, none of them wanted Croatian citizenship, and they were involved in an armed conflict and occupation of a state which the SFRY did not recognise. In those circumstances, we would submit, it is clear that they're enemy aliens, apart from the question of whether they had the right to apply for Croatian citizenship, and I'm not going to speak here about my own knowledge of what, in fact, happened subsequent to the armed conflict for those that wanted to acquire Croatian citizenship. But the Eritrea-Ethiopia case is actually far less forceful than this cases because those that were lawfully expelled were in fact dual citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm not now asking you to compare the one because that's the case you mentioned -- you referred to Lauterpacht when you referred to that case in your oral argument. I was just wondering whether the reference to that case, to Lauterpacht, which is, of course, already 14 years ago, that whether that would be the guiding principles, but you say this case is even stronger. That's clear. Then, finally, one question for Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic, you -- when arguing the -- the jurisdiction you said the following, and you were talking about armed conflict. You said: "As a matter of fact, in these cases," and you had referred to the IRA and the ETA, "they had a rather good hierarchical organisation. In some cases they even controlled parts of that territory. That is to say, there were some elements that could meet the criteria of customary international law that are applied for defining armed conflict." And then you said: "However, that never happened, and no international court ever established jurisdiction," which was then followed by, "and the jurisdiction of national courts was never brought into question." Your last remark suggests that if there's an armed conflict, that national courts would lose their jurisdiction because national courts - and that's perhaps my question to you - can exercise their jurisdiction, whether there exists or does not exist an armed conflict, of course, depending on what kind of cases they're dealing but that could include war crimes or crime against humanity. Would you agree with that or would you further explain what the last part of this sentence, "jurisdiction of national courts was never brought into question" what that exactly means in this context?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, I completely agree with your position and that was not my intention to provoke that questions [sic]. It is obviously that national courts has jurisdictions, no matter whether it's a context of the armed conflict or it's not. In fact, if the national courts did their duty in the very present case, I supposed we wouldn't be here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. We will conclude hearing this case at this moment. I wanted to join in the appreciation expressed by the parties already for the work done by all those who have assisted us; interpreters, technicians, transcribers, Registry. They've all made it possible to hear this case which kept us for quite a while in this and other courtrooms. I want to extend also on behalf of the Chamber my appreciation to the parties because a Chamber is limping and paralysed if it is not assisted by committed and dedicated parties which present their cases before the Chamber. It is to a large extent also because of the parties that a Chamber can perform its duties, and I would like to express my appreciation for that very specifically. I will adjourn in a minute. The Chamber is aware that there is a pending motion by the Gotovina Defence which doesn't need an immediate answer now. It will -- from what will follow, it will -- it can be concluded whether or not the Chamber has granted or has not granted that motion. The Chamber adjourns, sine die, and will deliver its Judgement in due course. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: sine die.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.53 p.m.,
